To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the phosphorylation state Rex-2 is a switch that determines the viral life-cycle, that phosphorylation of two serine residues in Rex is important for function, and that one or both serine residues are phosphorylated on threonine residues in Rex in vivo.

phosphorylation of two serine residues in human T-cell leukemia type 2 Rex is required for function, and the replacement of the two serine residues with phosphomimic aspartic acid residues restores Rex function.

(1) the phosphorylation of two serine residues in the C-terminal region of HTLV type-2 Rex is required for function; (2) the replacement of serine residues with phosphomimic aspartic acid residues restored function; (3) the replacement of both serine and threoenine residues with phospho-mimic aspartate residues restored Rex function; (4) the replacement of the serine and threoine residues with alanine resulted in decreased function
In summary, our research is concerned with
the function of a regulatory protein, called Rex, that is encoded by the human T-cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV).
the regulation of gene expression by the human T cell leukemia virus (HTL) type 2 Rex phosphoprotein and the role that phosphorylation plays in regulating Rex function.
understanding the molecular biology of human T-cell leukemia viruses, which cause a fatal T-cell lymphoproliferative disease in infected individuals.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the phosphorylation state Rex in the infected T-cell may be a switch which determines whether the virus is in a latent or productive state.
we have identified the first phosphorylation sites on the HTLV Rex protein.
phosphorylation of two serine residues in the Rex protein is required for Rex activity and Rex function is regulated by phosphorylation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phosphorylation of Rex is required for Rex function, and that phosphorylation on serines 151 and 152 is required for Rex to bind to its viral RNA.
phosphorylation of the HTLV-2 Rex protein regulates its function and that the phosphorylation state is important for the switch between latent and productive infection.
phosphorylation of Rex regulates its activity and that the phosphorylated form of Rex is the active form.
